title: Why SEK 200 billion of reserve borrowing would cut Sweden’s currency exposure by about SEK 100 billion
summary: The Riksbank’s Markets Department estimates that replacing roughly SEK 200 billion of reserve funding with foreign-currency loans would reduce the bank’s remaining currency exposure by around SEK 100 billion. The difference is an existing hedge. About half the prospective borrowing would replace FX swaps that already protect the balance sheet. The other half would be accompanied by outright sales of foreign currency for kronor. The distinction determines both the amount of incremental protection and the size of the prospective outright FX flow (pp. 2–3).

Currency risk is the bank’s largest financial exposure. The reserve was worth about SEK 450 billion at end-October. The dollar accounts for 70% of the asset allocation, the euro 17.5%, sterling and the Australian dollar 5% each, and the Norwegian krone 2.5%. Those are asset weights. Net exposures also depend on liabilities and swaps. Under the 2021 decision to phase out borrowing through the Debt Office, the bank held the foreign assets against liabilities denominated in kronor. In September 2023 it decided to hedge about one-quarter of the reserve with swaps. The two footnotes on page 2 date separate policy changes: how the assets were funded and how the resulting currency mismatch was managed.

The memorandum illustrates the scale with a sensitivity calculation. Despite the swaps, a general 20% krona appreciation would produce an estimated loss of approximately SEK 70 billion on the reserve, of which around SEK 48 billion relates to the dollar component. The dollar figure is part of the total. The premise is a broad appreciation. The historical observation motivating the exercise is narrower: the 12-month change in the krona’s rate against the dollar has at times exceeded 20%. Neither number gives the likelihood of a simultaneous move across the reserve currencies. The figures also describe the exposure before the proposed transaction. The department does not give a post-transaction loss estimate or the currency allocation of the planned borrowing (pp. 1–2).

Reserve managers face two different obligations. They must hold suitably low-risk, usable FX assets for lending foreign currency to banks, intervention and Sweden’s IMF obligations. The Riksbank must also be able to finance its operations. Matching an asset with a liability in the same currency reduces the sensitivity of its net krona value while preserving the foreign asset. This explains why a manager can favour less open currency exposure without advocating a smaller reserve. The alternative funding instrument introduces its own maturity and borrowing terms, which the memorandum leaves open. An exchange-rate hedge by itself tells a reserve manager little about when the cash to repay that debt falls due.

The implementation has consequences for krona liquidity as well as FX transactions. Under stable conditions the department envisages a 2027 start and a transition lasting 12 to 18 months. It would spread purchases of kronor over the period because they could influence the exchange rate. Both outright purchases and settlement of the old swaps would reduce the banking system’s liquidity surplus with the central bank by corresponding amounts. It would be a mistake to translate the entire decline in surplus into new outright purchases of kronor. Settlement of a hedge put on earlier and initiation of a new outright transaction have different implications for market flow. The size of any exchange-rate response is unspecified (pp. 2–3).

There is also a fiscal accounting effect. The Debt Office’s borrowing enters Maastricht gross debt, a measure whose perimeter excludes the Riksbank’s own gross debt. In a public-sector measure including both, the increase associated with the operation would be offset by the reduction in the central bank’s gross debt. A rise in the Maastricht measure would therefore say little by itself about new public spending or a change in the combined sector’s financing need. Chapter 10 of the Riksbank Act normally caps such borrowing at 5% of GDP at the decision date and permits larger, temporary borrowing in exceptional circumstances to strengthen reserves. The department anticipates a final decision and details in December. The exposure reduction, borrowing mix and timetable are preliminary assessments at 4 November (pp. 1–3).

questions.question: How sensitive would the reserve be to a dollar-only shock after the transition?
questions.detail: The memorandum quantifies the current dollar component of a broad appreciation stress, but the proposed SEK 100 billion reduction in exposure spans an unspecified set of currencies. Compare currency-level assets, hedges due to expire and new borrowing. A re-run of the bank’s stress with the resulting net positions would show how much dollar concentration remains.

questions.question: How do the dates of outright krona purchases compare with those of swap settlements?
questions.detail: Each leg amounts to about SEK 100 billion under the provisional plan. Their cash-flow calendars can differ considerably even if the programme proceeds at a smooth aggregate pace. Look for the Riksbank’s dealing arrangements and swap maturity disclosures alongside the Debt Office’s funding calendar. Together these could distinguish new outright purchases from expected settlements and identify concentrated dates.

questions.question: What refinancing exposure comes with the change in funding?
questions.detail: A currency-matched liability cushions valuation changes, but a short-dated loan funding longer-dated reserve assets can still require cash or refinancing under stress. Compare borrowing maturity, interest basis, collateral terms where relevant and the liquid assets held in each currency. The memorandum supplies neither a funding-cost comparison nor a maturity stress test.

questions.question: How much would the changing liquidity surplus matter to short-term rates?
questions.detail: The direction of the balance-sheet change is specified, while the marginal effect on money-market conditions depends on the starting surplus and its distribution. Check settlement balances, Riksbank liquidity operations and transaction-based overnight rates around actual settlement dates. Separate these cash movements from contemporaneous monetary policy announcements.
